lastAfter:
The Dohkar’s accusation still rang when I found my voice.

“It was not my doing. The girl took something I once told her in confidence and offered it to Fate on my behalf.”

The words left me thin. Every eye in the clearing pressed closer. The families who had come to witness their daughter’s First Sacrifice now stared at me as though the twist were my design. The youth knelt where the wish had taken her voice, hands at her throat, Weave-Script reduced to a single pale thread. She looked at me with the same startled hurt I felt.

A woman near the back—the one who had spoken the father’s name—stepped forward.

“You broke the seal. You heard what you wanted and let the rite twist to serve yourself.”

“I broke the seal to stop the twist,” I said. My voice carried farther than I meant. “The sacrifice no longer matched the desire. If I had stayed silent the cost would have fallen worse than this.”

Julian stood at the edge of the circle. His heel had stopped its restless tap against the root. Slate-hued gray-green eyes flecked with brighter green held on me, and for one breath I felt the pull of them the way I always did when he looked at me like that—like he was already weighing whether I would choose the truth that hurt or the silence that protected what little standing I still had.

The Dohkar raised a hand.

“The supervisor does not speak for the rite. She answers for it.”

Another voice rose from the families, sharp with fear for their own child’s future.

“She let the girl pay for her own missing father. That is not guidance. That is theft.”

I felt the weight of their certainty settle. If I kept explaining I would only sound more guilty. If I stayed silent the youth would carry the full blame and my own past would remain untouched. The choice sat between my teeth like a stone I could not swallow and could not spit out.

The clearing waited. No one moved. Even the spiralgrass seemed to hold its breath.

Present.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. I would ask Fate to make them believe me without me having to name the father I never knew. No. I would ask it to give the girl her voice back and leave me to answer for what I broke.

ringTail: The youth knelt on the crimson spiralgrass , her aqua skin luminous beneath the pale canopy. Her coral hair spilled forward as she drew breath to speak the offering we had rehearsed for months. "I give the discipline to finish my studies," she said, her voice steady. "I give the right to train as Sacrificiant." The words left her cleanly. I felt the alignment hold, a clean line through the clearing. My mouth stayed sealed beneath the gossamer band. Two dozen First Favored watched in silence, their Weave-Script shifting with quiet expectation. Julian stood at the edge; his heel tapped once against the root before he locked the motion. Then she looked at me. Her next breath hitched once, audible over the grass. Something shifted in her posture, a sudden reach. "I give it instead so she may find the father who left her," she said. The sentence landed like a stone in still water. The prepared sacrifice no longer matched the desire spoken. I felt the misalignment at once, a sour note through the air. Every First Favored present felt it too. The Dohkar presiding stiffened. A faint resin scent drifted from the cuff of his sleeve. The youth meant it as kindness. She had taken something I once let slip in private and offered it to Fate on my behalf. The taboo was absolute. No one was meant to wish upon another's First Sacrifice. A single leaf scraped along the spiralgrass and stopped against the youth's knee. The Weave-Script on the youth's skin flickered with sudden doubt. I could not speak. The band muffled everything. Protocol forbade interference. Yet if I stayed silent, the wish would twist in ways none of us could predict. The father I had never known would be pulled toward me by whatever path Fate chose, and the cost would fall on the girl kneeling before us. Julian's gaze met mine for one held moment. His stillness told me he saw the same fracture I did. I reached up and tore the gossamer band free. The cloth came away with a soft sound that carried farther than it should have. Every eye turned. The inference was immediate and obvious: the supervisor had broken her seal for a wish that named her. Manipulation. Ruin. The Dohkar's voice rose, sharp. "The rite is compromised." Fate answered before anyone could move farther. A guest near the back, a woman I had never spoken to, spoke the name of the man who had left me years ago. She said it as if remembering something she had not meant to voice aloud. The words hung in the air. The youth's face went slack with surprise. The wish had found its path through ordinary mouths and ordinary memory. The literal request stood fulfilled by coincidence that was not coincidence. The youth's hands flew to her throat. A sound tried to leave her and failed. Her Weave-Script dimmed to a single pale thread. The discipline she had offered was gone, and with it the voice she would have used to train. Fate had taken the one thing she had not named. The clearing erupted in whispers. Accusations followed. The supervisor had interfered. The rite had been turned for personal gain. My qualification as Dohkar hung by a thread. Julian stayed where he was. A low thread of his voice reached me when he cleared his throat once. He knew the truth of what had happened. He knew what it would cost me to explain it. The weight of their stares pressed closer. One more word from me and the suspicion would become certainty. Silence might preserve the fragile story I had built around my past, but it left the youth bearing the full price alone. Confess my truth and risk their rejection, or bury it deeper and let the silence suffocate me? I didn't remember bringing it. My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.
